nodes.label: Kirkpatrick's Four Levels
nodes.one_line: Place any evaluation question at the right level — reaction, learning, behavior, or results — instead of only ever measuring reaction.
know_what: Four levels — reaction, learning, behavior, results (Kirkpatrick), each answering a different evaluation question at increasing cost and difficulty to measure
Level 1: Reaction — whether participants found the training favorable, engaging, and relevant, typically measured with an end-of-session survey
Level 2: Learning — whether participants acquired the intended knowledge, skills, or attitude, typically measured with an assessment
Level 3: Behavior — whether participants apply what they learned back on the job, measured through observation, manager report, or performance data over time
Level 4: Results — whether the training produced a measurable organizational outcome, such as cost, quality, retention, or revenue, the hardest level to isolate and attribute
New World Kirkpatrick Model — a later revision emphasizing starting evaluation design at Level 4 and working backward, and adding 'leading indicators' at Level 3
know_how: Place a proposed evaluation question at the correct level before designing the instrument, since a Level 1 tool can't answer a Level 3 question
Design an evaluation plan starting from the Level 4 result the sponsor cares about and work backward to the Level 3 behaviors that would produce it
Choose an appropriately rigorous method for each level — a survey is sufficient for Level 1 but not for Level 3, which needs observation or job performance data
Set expectations with a sponsor about which levels a given evaluation budget and timeline can actually reach
Distinguish reaction data from learning data instead of treating a satisfied learner as evidence they learned anything
Identify leading indicators at Level 3 that predict Level 4 results, when full Level 4 attribution isn't feasible
habits: Ask which level a stakeholder's evaluation question actually belongs to before proposing a method
Resist reporting only Level 1 data as if it answered a Level 4 question
Start evaluation design from the business result and work backward, not the other way around
Flag when a sponsor's expectations exceed what the evaluation budget can actually measure
Check whether a claimed evaluation result is actually backed by data at the level it's being cited for

know_why.claim: Evaluation should always aim to reach Level 3 or 4, not stop at Level 1 reaction data.
know_why.because: reaction data measures satisfaction, not whether training actually changed behavior or produced a business result, and satisfaction is a weak predictor of either
know_why.disputed_by: practitioners who argue Level 3/4 evaluation is often prohibitively expensive and slow relative to its value, and that Robert Brinkerhoff's Success Case Method, sampling a few extreme cases in depth rather than measuring every learner, gets usable answers faster and cheaper
know_why.source: Kirkpatrick's Four Levels vs. Robert Brinkerhoff, The Success Case Method

nodes.checkpoint: Given three stakeholder evaluation questions, correctly place each at its Kirkpatrick level and propose a method appropriate to that level's rigor requirement.
nodes.common_failure: Reporting a high satisfaction score as evidence a training program worked, when satisfaction (Level 1) has been repeatedly shown to correlate weakly with actual behavior change or business results.
sources: Donald & James Kirkpatrick, Four Levels of Training Evaluation
James & Wendy Kirkpatrick, the New World Kirkpatrick Model
Robert Brinkerhoff, The Success Case Method

nodes.label: Data Collection Instrument Design
nodes.one_line: Design a survey or observation instrument that measures the outcome you actually care about, not just what's easy to ask.
know_what: Survey item design — writing a question that measures one thing at a time, avoiding double-barreled and leading phrasing
Likert scale — an ordinal agreement scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, used for attitude and reaction measurement, with known pitfalls such as central tendency bias and acquiescence bias
Observation protocol — a structured checklist or rubric used to record behavior directly rather than relying on self-report
Response rate and non-response bias — the risk that only a skewed subset of the population responds to a voluntary instrument, distorting the results
Mixed methods — combining quantitative instruments, such as surveys, with qualitative ones, such as interviews and open-ended questions, to capture what a single method type would miss
Piloting an instrument — testing a draft survey or observation protocol on a small sample before full deployment to catch confusing items or missing response options
know_how: Write survey items that ask about one thing at a time, avoiding double-barreled questions that conflate two variables
Choose an observation protocol over self-report when the goal is measuring actual behavior rather than perceived behavior
Design for an adequate response rate, with a clear purpose statement, reasonable length, and appropriate timing, and check for non-response bias in the results
Combine a quantitative instrument with a small set of open-ended or interview questions when the evaluation question needs both breadth and depth
Pilot a new instrument with a small sample and revise confusing items before full deployment
Match instrument type to Kirkpatrick level — a survey fits Level 1, an observation protocol or work-sample review fits Level 3
habits: Read each survey item and ask whether it's actually measuring one specific thing
Pilot an instrument before trusting it at scale, even under time pressure
Check response rate and think about who might be missing from it before trusting a result
Reach for an observation protocol instead of a self-report survey when the question is about actual behavior
Match the instrument type to the actual Kirkpatrick level being measured, not to what's fastest to build
nodes.checkpoint: Design a data collection instrument matched to a stated evaluation question and Kirkpatrick level, pilot it with at least three respondents, and revise at least one item based on pilot feedback.
nodes.common_failure: Reusing a generic satisfaction survey template for every evaluation question regardless of what's actually being measured, producing Level 1 data dressed up to answer a Level 3 or 4 question.
sources: Jack Phillips, Measuring ROI in Training and Development
Michael Quinn Patton, mixed-methods evaluation guidance

nodes.label: LMS Analytics Reading
nodes.one_line: Read LMS completion, time-on-task, and drop-off data well enough to tell a real design problem from noise.
know_what: Completion rate — the proportion of enrolled learners who finish a course, a coarse metric that says nothing about quality without more context
Time-on-task — how long a learner spends on a given screen or module, useful for spotting content that's confusingly slow or suspiciously fast, a sign of skipping
Drop-off point — the specific screen or module where the largest proportion of learners exit without completing, often more diagnostic than the overall completion rate
xAPI statement — a granular activity record such as 'learner X attempted Y with result Z', providing richer behavioral data than SCORM's completion-only tracking

Confounded metric — a metric whose interpretation depends on unstated context, since a low completion rate could mean bad content or a mandatory-but-ignored assignment, which needs a second data source to disambiguate
Dashboard literacy — reading an LMS or xAPI dashboard critically, distinguishing what it actually measures from what a stakeholder might assume it measures
know_how: Pull completion, time-on-task, and drop-off data for a course and identify the specific module where the largest drop-off occurs
Cross-reference a suspiciously short time-on-task with content difficulty to distinguish rapid mastery from skipping
Use xAPI statement-level data instead of SCORM completion-only data when the evaluation question needs behavioral detail SCORM can't provide
Pair a confounded LMS metric with a second data source, such as a survey or interview, before drawing a conclusion from it alone
Explain to a sponsor what a specific dashboard metric does and doesn't measure, correcting an assumption before it drives a wrong decision
Compare analytics across cohorts or time periods to distinguish a one-time anomaly from a persistent pattern
habits: Ask what a metric doesn't measure before reporting what it does
Go straight to the drop-off point instead of stopping at the overall completion rate
Check a surprising time-on-task number against content difficulty before interpreting it
Pair a quantitative LMS metric with a qualitative source before drawing a conclusion
Distinguish a confounded metric from a clean one before letting it drive a design decision on its own
nodes.checkpoint: Given raw LMS completion and time-on-task data for a course, identify the specific module with the highest drop-off and propose one plausible, testable explanation for it.
nodes.common_failure: Reporting an overall completion rate as the headline evaluation metric without looking at module-level drop-off data, which hides exactly where and why learners are disengaging.
sources: xAPI (Experience API / Tin Can API) specification
Will Thalheimer, learning analytics critique and guidance

nodes.label: Level 3 Transfer Measurement
nodes.one_line: Measure whether a skill actually transferred to the job, not just whether the learner passed the course.
know_what: Transfer of training — whether a skill learned in training is actually applied on the job, the specific thing Level 3 measures
Transfer climate — the workplace conditions, such as manager support, opportunity to apply, and resource availability, that determine whether transfer happens regardless of how good the training was
Manager reinforcement — the specific, documented practice of a manager following up on training application, one of the strongest predictors of whether transfer occurs
Self-report vs. observed transfer — a learner's own account of applying a skill versus a manager's or observer's independent account, which frequently diverge
Time lag for measurement — Level 3 transfer typically needs weeks to months to observe, unlike Level 1 or 2 which can be measured immediately
Barriers to transfer — specific, nameable obstacles, such as no opportunity to use the skill, conflicting incentives, or lack of tools, distinct from a simple 'the training didn't work' conclusion
know_how: Design a Level 3 measurement with an appropriate time lag, typically four to twelve weeks post-training, instead of measuring immediately
Collect both self-report and manager or observer data on transfer and compare them, rather than relying on self-report alone
Assess transfer climate alongside the transfer measurement itself, since climate often explains a low transfer result better than the training's quality does
Interview a sample of managers about specific instances of application, not just a general 'did they apply it' rating
Identify named barriers to transfer when transfer is low, distinguishing a training problem from an environment problem
Use a manager reinforcement checklist or nudge as an intervention paired with the training itself, since reinforcement measurably increases transfer
habits: Wait the appropriate time lag before measuring transfer instead of checking too soon
Collect manager or observer data alongside self-report, not instead of digging deeper
Check transfer climate before concluding a low transfer result means the training failed
Ask for a specific instance of application, not a general rating, when interviewing about transfer
Distinguish a training problem from a transfer-climate problem before recommending a fix
nodes.checkpoint: Design and run a Level 3 transfer measurement for a completed training program, including both self-report and manager-observed data collected after an appropriate time lag, and identify at least one specific barrier to transfer if transfer is low.
nodes.common_failure: Measuring transfer immediately after training with a self-report-only survey, which produces an inflated and unreliable picture of whether the skill is actually being used on the job weeks later.
sources: Timothy Baldwin & J. Kevin Ford, transfer of training research
Mary Broad & John Newstrom, Transfer of Training

nodes.label: ROI & Business Case Building
nodes.one_line: Build the business case that connects training spend to a measurable organizational outcome a sponsor cares about.
know_what: ROI formula (Phillips) — program benefits minus program costs, divided by program costs, expressed as a percentage, used to express training's return in financial terms
Isolating the effect of training — separating training's contribution to a result from other factors, such as a process change, a market shift, or a new tool, that happened at the same time
Converting data to monetary value — translating a non-financial outcome, such as fewer errors or faster onboarding, into a dollar figure using a defensible, documented method
Fully loaded cost — the total cost of a training program including design, development, delivery time, and participant opportunity cost, not just the visible line-item cost
Intangible benefits — real outcomes, such as morale, brand reputation, or retention, that resist reliable monetary conversion and should be reported alongside ROI, not forced into it
Business case — a forward-looking proposal justifying investment in a training program before it's built, distinct from an ROI calculation, which is typically done after the fact
know_how: Calculate fully loaded program cost, including development time and participant opportunity cost, not just the visible delivery budget
Apply an isolation technique, such as a control group, a trend-line extrapolation, or expert estimation with a confidence discount, to separate training's effect from other contributing factors
Convert a measured outcome to monetary value using a documented, defensible method, and state the assumptions behind the conversion openly
Report intangible benefits separately from the ROI percentage instead of forcing a rough monetary estimate onto something that resists it
Build a forward-looking business case using estimated costs and projected benefits when justifying a program before it exists, distinct from a retrospective ROI calculation
Present ROI results with the isolation and conversion assumptions visible, so a skeptical stakeholder can see exactly what the number does and doesn't account for
habits: State the isolation method and its limitations whenever presenting an ROI figure
Use fully loaded cost, not just the visible line-item budget, in any ROI calculation
Keep intangible benefits in the report as their own category instead of squeezing them into a shaky dollar estimate
Show the assumptions behind a monetary conversion instead of just presenting the final number
Distinguish a retrospective ROI calculation from a forward-looking business case, and use the right one for the audience's actual decision

know_why.claim: Training's ROI should be calculated and reported as a specific percentage figure.
know_why.because: sponsors and finance stakeholders think in financial terms, and a credible ROI number secures budget and demonstrates accountability in that language
know_why.disputed_by: evaluation practitioners who argue the isolation and monetary-conversion steps require so many soft assumptions that a precise-looking ROI percentage often overstates its own certainty, and prefer reporting a range or qualitative business case instead of a single number
know_why.source: Jack Phillips, ROI Methodology, vs. evaluation-rigor critiques, including from the American Evaluation Association, of over-precise causal claims in organizational evaluation

nodes.checkpoint: Build a business case or ROI report for one training program with fully loaded costs, a stated isolation method, a documented monetary conversion for at least one outcome, and intangible benefits reported separately.
nodes.common_failure: Presenting an ROI percentage without stating the isolation method or conversion assumptions behind it, which collapses under the first skeptical question from a finance stakeholder.
sources: Patricia Pulliam Phillips, business case development
American Evaluation Association guidance on causal claims

nodes.label: Continuous Improvement Cycle
nodes.one_line: Turn pilot and evaluation data into a scheduled revision instead of a course that ships once and calcifies.
know_what: Continuous improvement cycle — a scheduled, recurring loop of collect data, analyze, revise, and redeploy, applied to a live program rather than a one-time launch evaluation
PDSA cycle (Plan-Do-Study-Act) — a lightweight, repeatable improvement framework adapted from quality management into ongoing program revision
Revision backlog — a prioritized, tracked list of known issues and improvement ideas for a live program, reviewed on a set cadence instead of acted on ad hoc
Version history — a record of what changed in a program across revision cycles and why, which prevents re-litigating a decision already made and reversed once

Trigger for off-cycle revision — a defined threshold, such as a sudden completion-rate drop or a critical content error, that justifies an unscheduled fix rather than waiting for the next scheduled cycle
Sunset criteria — a stated condition under which a program gets retired or fully redesigned rather than incrementally revised, since not every problem is fixable through iteration
know_how: Set a recurring cadence, such as quarterly or per-cohort, for reviewing evaluation data and deciding on revisions, rather than only revising when something breaks visibly
Maintain a prioritized revision backlog fed by pilot findings, evaluation data, and facilitator feedback
Log each revision with what changed and why, building a version history that prevents re-debating settled decisions
Define a threshold that triggers an off-cycle emergency revision, distinct from the regular cadence
Apply a lightweight PDSA cycle to test a proposed revision on a small scale before rolling it out to the full program
Set sunset criteria for a program up front, so a program past its useful life gets retired deliberately instead of endlessly patched
habits: Check the revision backlog on the scheduled cadence, not just when something breaks
Log why a change was made, not just what changed
Test a revision at small scale before rolling it out everywhere
Ask whether a program has quietly crossed its own sunset criteria
Review evaluation data against the sunset criteria on schedule, not only when a program is already visibly failing
nodes.checkpoint: Set up a revision backlog and a scheduled review cadence for a live program, log at least one prior revision with its rationale, and define both an off-cycle trigger and a sunset criterion.
nodes.common_failure: Treating a course as finished at launch and only revisiting it when a stakeholder complains loudly, instead of running a scheduled review cycle that catches smaller problems before they compound.
sources: ATD guidance on program lifecycle management
Michael Allen, Leaving ADDIE for SAM
